Idris stands in the field by his house, listening to his niece's question. The family is all around him—Wren, Corwin, Liora. No food in the house. He knew this before he woke, foresters always know when the larder's thin.

Forty years ago Nell Holloway told him she moved the boundary marker between her orchard and his nephew's field. Asked him to stay quiet about it. He promised. Forty years he's kept it, watching Wren lose sleep over it now, unable to speak the one sentence that would end the quarrel.

He cuts wood for both households. Has for decades. Never asked why the two houses can't share space like they share heat.

"Corwin." He names his nephew full. "Forest with me."

The boy needs work, needs to be somewhere else, and Idris needs another pair of hands to fell what will warm both houses through the winter. The marker business can wait. Winter won't. Idris gives no other word. The forest is where he's needed, and Corwin with him. What Liora asked about food, what Wren carries quiet—those are problems for later in the day, after timber is cut and the winter stores begin to fill.
